extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism; students of English literature; aspiring novelists and diarists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the implicit criteria this essay uses to judge fiction (novels and plays) and diary/narrative writing — e.g., simplicity of style, suitability of plan, characterization, narrative interest, liveliness of description, and the author's impartiality. Useful for assessing creative prose in the 18th‑century realist tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as an attractive quality
rubrics_metrics.description: “It wanted something of the simplicity which had been among the most attractive charms of Evelina.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity of manner and tone is presented as a positive virtue in fiction; losing that simplicity (even while gaining other merits) can lessen a work’s charm. Example: Evelina’s simplicity contrasted with Cecilia’s greater complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan suited to the writer’s strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: “She determined to write a new tale, on a plan excellently contrived for the display of the powers in which her superiority to other writers lay.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work should be designed to showcase the particular talents of its author — choose a structure/plan that permits the author’s strengths to operate effectively (e.g., a gallery of characters to show character-drawing skill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and striking characterization (distinctive features)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A grand and various picture-gallery, which presented to the eye a long series of men and women, each marked by some strong peculiar feature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong fiction often contains a wide cast whose members are clearly differentiated by vivid, identifiable traits (avarice, prodigality, garrulity, silence, etc.). Distinctive character traits help make characters memorable and the social panorama convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative interest and unity over mere wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on The Witlings: “the piece had abundance of wit but no interest, that it was bad as a whole.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleverness or wit alone does not make a successful dramatic piece (or story); the work must sustain overall interest and cohere as a whole. Patching blemishes may be insufficient if the piece lacks an underlying engaging purpose or dramatic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and avoiding unduly close imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: “It would remind every reader of the Femmes Savantes, which, strange to say, she had never read, and that she could not sustain so close a comparison with Moliere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work that closely recalls a famous predecessor risks unfavorable comparison; strive for originality of handling and voice rather than recreating a recognizable model too closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liveliness and picturesque quality in diary/narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: “The portion of the Diary which relates to this celebrated proceeding is lively and picturesque.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal or historical narrative benefits from vivid, picturesque detail and lively reporting — these qualities make diary passages valuable to readers and historians alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative/description excellence in reporting events
rubrics_metrics.description: “The account which she has given of the King’s illness contains much excellent narrative and description.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, well-told narrative and careful descriptive detail are marks of high-quality diary or reportorial writing; they increase historical and literary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-awareness and appropriate tone in private writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Her Diary “recorded with minute diligence all the compliments... for the eyes of two or three persons who had loved her from infancy... Nothing can be more unjust than to confound these outpourings of a kind heart... with the egotism of a bluestocking.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private or semi-private writing should be read with attention to intended audience and tone — intimacy and the recording of compliments for a small circle is not necessarily egotism. Authors should be conscious of whom they are writing for and modulate tone accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain critical judgement and avoid partisan bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay criticizes how Court life made her espouse causes with “presumptuous vehemence and acrimony,” showing that her powers of reasoning and sense of justice were impaired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers, even diarists recounting events, should preserve impartiality and informed judgment rather than allowing social affiliation or environment to cloud their assessment; partisan or unexamined allegiance can weaken credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic growth and demonstration of matured powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Cecilia: “it furnished ample proof that the four years, which had elapsed since Evelina appeared, had not been unprofitably spent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A later work should show evidence of the author’s development and refinement of craft; improvement over earlier works is a positive sign of artistic growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints of authorial life affect output
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that service in the royal household made it “impossible for her to write” and that the King said “She has given up five years of her pen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works with awareness of the author’s circumstances: external duties and life choices can limit an author’s productive capacity and influence the form and frequency of their output; this context matters when judging career trajectories or unevenness in output.
